answer.rationale: Rollback is ruled out by compliance (security patch must stay), so memory_b1's precedent is unusable regardless of how well it worked on day 18. The degradation is confined to the primary region while the release is presumably global, which weakens the release-as-cause hypothesis and favors a region-scoped fault (host, storage, or primary-region write capacity). That points at regional_failover, and memory_b2 is the closest precedent, so I want its original record to check whether the March degradation was also write-heavy and write-path confined or whether it was a read/latency event that shifted cleanly for reasons that will not hold under peak settlement writes. Failover during heavy writes is exactly where in-flight writes get lost, which is the one thing the objective forbids, so the scale is a small guarded test: shift a bounded slice of write traffic with drain-and-confirm before any broader cut. I also want memory_b3 because add_capacity is the plausible alternative if the primary region is simply saturated at settlement peak; b3's record will tell me whether headroom was provisioned in advance (which would not transfer to a 90-minute in-flight incident) or added live. Circuit breakers (b4) fail fast, which sheds the customer writes I am trying to preserve, and read replicas (b5) address read load on the primary, which is only relevant if dashboard or report queries are actually contributing here, and nothing in the current signal says they are. Downstream risk: these memories are consolidated summaries of successes, and I cannot see the base rate of failed failovers or the conditions that made each one clean, so a confident-sounding precedent may be encoding survivorship. If verification shows b2's success depended on conditions absent today, I switch to add_capacity rather than force the failover.
